name: Clostebol (4-chlorotestosterone)

lead: Clostebol is a testosterone derivative with a chlorine atom added. It is sold in some countries as a topical wound-healing product and has been used as a steroid ester.
It shows up mainly in doping news. No studies test it for muscle or appearance.

paras: It is an androgen-receptor agonist. The chlorine is said to stop conversion to DHT and oestrogen. Its anabolic effect is described as modest.
Risks are inferred from anabolic steroids in general; clostebol-specific human safety data for physique use are lacking. It is prohibited in sport and controlled in the US, Canada and Brazil.

lead: Clostebol, also called 4-chlorotestosterone, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from testosterone by adding a chlorine atom at the 4-position. It is usually formulated as an ester such as clostebol acetate, caproate or propionate [1][2].

Its main legitimate uses are topical: clostebol acetate has been used in dermatological and ophthalmological products, and in some countries, including Italy, creams and sprays containing it are sold for skin wounds [1]. It is prohibited at all times by the World Anti-Doping Agency and appears regularly in doping cases, some of them attributed to accidental transdermal contamination [1][3][4].
No clinical trials have tested clostebol for appearance or physique. The published literature on it is dominated by anti-doping analysis.
infobox: US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV; Brazil Class C5; WADA-prohibited

paras: Clostebol acetate is used topically for infected or slowly healing skin lesions in some countries, often in combination with an antibiotic such as neomycin under the brand Trofodermin [1]. Historical medical use of systemic forms has been reported for conditions such as osteoporosis, anorexia and wasting [2]. It has also been used illicitly as a growth promoter in cattle, which has led to residue surveillance [2].

The chlorine substituent is said to block conversion to dihydrotestosterone and to oestrogens [1]. Grokipedia gives an anabolic-to-androgenic ratio of about 46:25 relative to testosterone's 100:100 [2], whereas Wikipedia describes clostebol as a weak anabolic steroid [1]. Studies have characterised its urinary sulfate metabolites in a Caucasian population [5] and new metabolites for doping control [6].

No studies found of clostebol for appearance or physique. Human research is analytical, including a study of detectability in urine after transdermal application of clostebol and several other anabolic steroids [7] and reviews of how clostebol positives in sport may arise from accidental exposure [4].

Wikipedia lists numerous athletes suspended for clostebol, including baseball players Freddy Galvis and Dee Gordon, skier Therese Johaug and footballer Jose Luis Palomino [1]. In 2024 tennis player Jannik Sinner tested positive; the International Tennis Integrity Agency found contamination from his physiotherapist's use of a clostebol-containing spray on a cut, and after a WADA case resolution agreement he served a three-month ban in 2025 [1]. A 2020 review asked whether many detections reflect accidental doping [4].
